summary: MPL provides IPv6 multicast forwarding in low-power, lossy networks without building or maintaining any multicast tree. Messages are disseminated to all forwarders in an MPL domain using the Trickle algorithm. This standards-track RFC defines the protocol and its two operating modes, one that is proactive and one that is reactive.

plainLanguage.summary: In a crowd of tiny sensors, news spreads by everyone repeating it a few times to their neighbors. Nobody needs a map, and the message still reaches everyone.

questions: multicast for low power lossy networks
multicast protocol for low power lossy networks
how does mpl use the trickle algorithm
subtitle: Multicast for tiny wireless networks: every node repeats new messages a few times using Trickle, and nobody builds a multicast tree.

tldr.problem: Low-power and lossy networks (LLNs) have little memory and unstable wireless links, so building and maintaining a multicast routing topology is too costly or not feasible.
tldr.mechanism: MPL floods multicast messages to every MPL Forwarder in an MPL Domain, using the Trickle algorithm to schedule transmissions. Proactive forwarding repeats new messages a limited number of times, and reactive forwarding uses MPL Control Messages to find neighbors that are missing messages.
tldr.outcome: Forwarders need no multicast routes and keep small, constant state for each seed that sends messages. The RFC states that MPL has no built-in cryptographic security and relies on link-layer security.

today: RFC 7731 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC, so it is still the definition of MPL.

sections.title: Multicast Without a Tree
sections.content:
Normal IP multicast routing builds and maintains a topology that reaches every subscriber of a group. In a low-power and lossy network that is costly. Devices may only have memory for links to a few neighbors, and the dynamic nature of wireless links makes the upkeep expensive. Some mechanisms also need two-hop topology information, and the cost of maintaining it grows polynomially with network density.

The Multicast Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (MPL) avoids building any multicast routing topology. It disseminates multicast messages to all MPL Forwarders in an MPL Domain. By using the Trickle algorithm from RFC 6206, it needs only small, constant state for each device that starts disseminations, and the communication rate scales logarithmically with density.

Although designed for LLNs, MPL may be used in any network where no multicast routing state is wanted. A host does not need to know that MPL is in use if its attachment router forwards multicast between the MPL Domain and the host.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets cannot keep a big map of who needs which message. So MPL skips the map and has everyone pass the message along a few times.

sections.title: Domains, Seeds and Forwarders
sections.content:
An MPL Forwarder is a router that runs MPL. An MPL Domain is a scope zone (as in RFC 4007) whose interfaces subscribe to the same MPL Domain Address. An MPL Seed is a forwarder that creates MPL Data Messages and acts as the entry point into the domain; each seed has an MPL Seed Identifier that is unique within the domain.

The default Domain Address is the ALL_MPL_FORWARDERS multicast address with Realm-Local scope (scop value 3). A forwarder in several domains can use that address for at most one of them, and every other domain MUST have its own unique address. Where scopes span subnets of different technologies, Admin-Local (4) or Site-Local (5) scope SHOULD be used.

Each forwarder keeps an information base. The Seed Set records, per seed, a lower-bound sequence number (MinSequence) and a lifetime; messages below the bound are ignored. The Buffered Message Set holds recent data messages from each seed, all at or above MinSequence. There are also a Local Interface Set and a Domain Set.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain is like a neighborhood group chat. The seed is whoever posts a new message, and each message gets a number so everyone can tell if they have already seen it.

sections.title: How a Message Spreads
sections.content:
When a seed has a multicast message to send, it makes an MPL Data Message: the Domain Address as the IPv6 destination, its Seed Identifier, a new sequence number and the message. If the original destination is not the Domain Address, the message is wrapped by IPv6-in-IPv6 tunneling (RFC 2473), preserving the original destination.

A forwarder that receives a data message checks the sequence number against the Seed Set and the Buffered Message Set. If the number is below the lower bound or the message is already buffered, it is old. Otherwise it is new: the forwarder updates its sets, processes the payload and multicasts the message a number of times on its MPL interfaces in the domain.

Two strategies can run together. With proactive forwarding, new messages are retransmitted on a Trickle schedule without any sign that neighbors need them, and the forwarder stops after a limited number of transmissions. With reactive forwarding, forwarders send link-local MPL Control Messages on a Trickle schedule summarizing which messages they hold; a neighbor that sees something missing schedules those data messages for transmission. The default parameters combine both.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who hears a new message repeats it a few times. Now and then neighbors also compare notes, and if one is missing something, it gets passed along.

sections.title: Parameters and Defaults
sections.content:
MPL is tuned with a handful of parameters. PROACTIVE_FORWARDING defaults to TRUE. SEED_SET_ENTRY_LIFETIME defaults to 30 minutes; a value that is too small can break duplicate detection, so a forwarder may receive the same message more than once.

Data messages and control messages each have their own Trickle settings: the minimum interval (Imin), the maximum interval (Imax), the redundancy constant k and a fourth parameter this RFC adds, TimerExpirations, the number of timer expiration events before Trickle is stopped for a message. Setting the control message TimerExpirations to 0 turns reactive forwarding off, and no control messages are sent.

All interfaces on the same link of a domain are RECOMMENDED to use the same Trickle values, since Trickle may behave unexpectedly otherwise. The RFC does not say how these parameters are set. Setting DATA_MESSAGE_IMAX equal to DATA_MESSAGE_IMIN is acceptable in the default case, since later retransmissions are triggered by control messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Settings control how often and how many times to repeat. If everybody uses different settings, the crowd gets confused, so neighbors should agree.

sections.title: MPL Option and Control Message
sections.content:
Data messages carry the MPL Option, an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option placed right after the IPv6 header, with option type 0x6D. Its flags are S (2 bits, the size of the seed-id), M (1 bit, set when the sequence number is known to be the largest received from the seed) and V (1 bit, 0 for this specification; messages with V set to 1 MUST be dropped), followed by 4 reserved bits, an 8-bit sequence and the optional seed-id. When S is 0 the seed-id is the IPv6 source address and is left out. Nodes that do not understand the option MUST discard the message. Sequence values are compared using Serial Number Arithmetic (RFC 1982).

The MPL Control Message is an ICMPv6 message of type 159 and code 0, sent with a hop limit of 255 to the link-scoped Domain Address. It contains a list of MPL Seed Info entries, one per entry in the Seed Set. Each holds an 8-bit min-seqno, a 6-bit bm-len, a 2-bit S, the seed-id and a bit-vector in which bit i says whether sequence number min-seqno + i is in the sender's buffer. Control message size grows linearly with the number of simultaneous seeds, at 4 octets per seed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a small label saying who started it and its number. The 'compare notes' message is a checklist of the numbers a node already has.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
For each data message it is actively forwarding, a forwarder MUST run a separate Trickle timer. A transmission is "consistent" when it receives a data message with the same domain address, seed-id and sequence value. It is "inconsistent" when the message has the M flag set and a lower sequence value. After DATA_MESSAGE_TIMER_EXPIRATIONS events the timer MUST be disabled, and the message may then be dropped by advancing MinSequence.

On receiving a data message, a forwarder either accepts it into the buffer, accepts it and moves MinSequence to one above its sequence number, or discards it. It MUST discard messages below MinSequence or already buffered. When accepted, it resets the seed entry's lifetime, starts a Trickle timer for the message if proactive forwarding is on, and starts or resets the control message timer. If memory is limited it SHOULD reclaim space by advancing MinSequence or deleting expired seed entries.

For control messages, one Trickle timer runs per domain. A forwarder compares a neighbor's bit-vector to its own. If it is missing something the neighbor has, or the neighbor is missing something it holds, it MUST reset the control timer, and for messages the neighbor lacks it also resets the data message timer and the expiration counter.
sections.plainLanguage: Each node writes down which numbered messages it has seen and ignores repeats. When a neighbor's checklist shows a gap, the node starts passing messages along again.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA allocated three things for MPL. The first is the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop option type 0x6D, named MPL Option. The value 0x4D, previously used for the MPL Option, has been marked Deprecated. The second is ICMPv6 type 159, named MPL Control Message. The third is a well-known multicast address, ALL_MPL_FORWARDERS, written FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:0:FC and registered on 2013-04-10 from the Variable Scope Multicast Addresses registry.

The high-order bits of the option type are set to 011, so nodes that do not understand the option discard the packet, and the option data (the M flag) may change as the message is forwarded.
sections.plainLanguage: MPL got its own official labels: one for the message tag, one for the 'compare notes' message and one shared group address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MPL has no cryptographic security of its own. The RFC notes that being able to inject messages into an LLN can be used for denial of service whatever the forwarding protocol, and because MPL disseminates messages, a spoofed message can affect a whole MPL Domain. LLNs usually rely on link-layer security, such as the IEEE 802.15.4 frame security that uses AES-128. If attackers can get access to the LLN, MPL SHOULD NOT be used.

The sequence numbers create a specific weakness. An attacker can spoof a message with a sufficiently large sequence number, which flushes the Buffered Message Set and raises MinSequence for that seed. Forwarding of messages in progress then stops, and new messages from the seed are not accepted until their sequence numbers pass MinSequence or the Seed Set entry expires. This applies to both proactive and reactive modes.

A forwarder MUST NOT accept or forward data messages from an interface that does not subscribe to the Domain Address in the message's destination. The security considerations of Trickle (RFC 6206) also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could shout a huge number and make everyone think they have already seen all the real messages, so protect the network and keep strangers out.

items.title: Proactive forwarding
items.text: Retransmits each new data message on a Trickle schedule, with no sign that neighbors need it, then stops after a limited number of transmissions.

items.title: Reactive forwarding
items.text: Sends MPL Control Messages on a Trickle schedule and retransmits only the data messages a neighbor is found to be missing.

fields.name: Opt Data Len
fields.desc: Length of the Option Data field in octets.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Set when the sequence is known to be the largest received from the seed.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: 0 for this specification; 1 means the message MUST be dropped.

fields.name: sequence
fields.desc: Relative ordering of messages from the seed.

items.label: Source address
items.desc: The seed-id is the IPv6 source address and is not included.

items.label: 16 bits
items.desc: The seed-id is a 16-bit unsigned integer.

items.desc: The seed-id is a 64-bit unsigned integer.

items.desc: The seed-id is a 128-bit unsigned integer.
